column1: # orgami's catalogue of third parties, and the committed evidence that proves an
# organization uses one. Nothing here is fetched, priced or authenticated: this
# file only knows what a vendor looks like when it appears in someone's code.
# Tab separated, one row per vendor:
#   id        the node id in the graph, as `vendor:<id>`
#   name      what a person calls it
#   category  the job it does. Two vendors sharing a category are two vendors
#             doing the same job, which is the question `orgami advise` asks —
#             so the value is load-bearing. Reuse an existing word rather than
#             coining a synonym, or the overlap goes unseen. Whether two vendors
#             sharing a category is worth *proposing* something about is advice
#             policy and lives in lib/advise.jq, not here: hosting and database
#             hold vendors that coexist on purpose, error-tracking and workspace
#             hold substitutes. That judgement changes; what a vendor looks like
#   signals   a `|`-separated list of `<kind>:<regex>`. A `|` only starts a new
#             signal when the text after it is one of the known kinds followed
#             by a colon, so a regex is free to use alternation of its own. The
#             list of known kinds lives in VENDOR_SIGNAL_KINDS in lib/vendors.sh
#             and nowhere else — a kind that is not in it is not rejected, it is
#             swallowed into the regex before it, and the vendor quietly stops
#   portal    where a human goes to see what it costs. Never opened by orgami.
#   flags     optional, comma separated, and absent from most rows — a row with
#             nothing to say here simply ends after `portal` rather than
#             carrying a trailing tab nobody can see. One flag is defined:
#               no-sdk  this vendor is normally wired in through a webhook URL,
#                       a script tag, or a variable the platform injects into
#                       the build itself. There is no package to install, so an
#                       environment variable that no dependency manifest backs
#                       up is the finished integration rather than an abandoned
#                       one, and `ghost-env-var` in lib/advise.jq skips the
#                       vendor entirely. This is not a flag for a vendor that
#                       has a real SDK people install and *also* happens to
#                       offer a webhook: Sentry and Stripe do not get it. Slack
#                       and Google Analytics do, because a webhook URL and a
#                       script tag are how they are actually integrated.
# The kinds, and what a fact of each one is:
#   pkg     a name in a dependency manifest        \
#   env     a variable name in a committed .env     |  read out of committed
#   host    a hostname in a literal URL             |  files by lib/vendors.sh
#   tf      a terraform provider                    |  during `orgami scan`
#   mx      a mail exchanger for the apex          \
#   spf     an SPF `include:` or `redirect=` target |  read out of public DNS
#   txt     a TXT record on the apex                |  by lib/dns.sh during
#   cname   a CNAME target on a conventional name   |  `orgami dns`
#   ns      a nameserver for the apex               |
# The two sets never mix. A signal only matches a fact of its own kind, so a
# `host:` regex can never be satisfied by a CNAME, and code and DNS stay two
# independent pieces of evidence for the same vendor rather than one restated.
# Code names what an organization *calls*. DNS names what it has an *account*
# with — a verification token is a vendor stating that this organization proved
# it owns this domain, which is the closest thing to a receipt anything here can
# see. That is why Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Greenhouse and DocuSign have
# rows at all: no repository will ever mention them.
# The regex is matched against the whole fact — an unanchored one is a substring
# test. `pkg:^stripe$` is the package called exactly `stripe`; `env:STRIPE_` is
# any variable with STRIPE_ in the name, which is how NEXT_PUBLIC_STRIPE_KEY and
# VITE_STRIPE_KEY are caught without a row each.
# Why the host signals still work. `lib/scan.sh` carries a NOISE_DOMAINS list
# that keeps registries and documentation domains — sentry.io among them — out
# of the `host:` nodes, because a link to a vendor's docs is not a deployment.
# That filter is deliberate and stays. `lib/vendors.sh` never applies it: it
# reads the URLs itself and matches them against this file, and what it emits is
# a `vendor:` node, not a `host:` one. So sentry.io is still suppressed as a
# host and still detected as a vendor, and the two lists never have to agree.
# Signals are evidence of use, not of a paid plan. Meilisearch, Grafana and
# Elastic all run self-hosted, and a `pkg` match cannot tell the difference —
# the graph says the code reaches for this vendor, and stops there.
